video_title: Trend Following Is Becoming Something Bigger Than Crisis Alpha | Systematic Investor | Ep.413
gist: In this Systematic Investor roundtable, Andrew Beer and Tom Roble argue trend following should be repositioned from a lumpy 'crisis alpha' hedge into a continuous all-weather allocation by raising its Sharpe ratio, while using a $45B AI fund's near-collapse and deep survivorship bias in the flagship CTA index to warn allocators about leverage, manager selection, and index illusions.

insights.claim: The trend barometer tracked by the hosts fell to 27%, meaning only about a quarter of the markets it monitors are in a trending state, signaling a historically narrow opportunity set for trend followers even as absolute year-to-date performance stays positive.
insights.speaker: Niels (host)
insights.so_what: A low trend-breadth reading is a leading indicator that CTA return dispersion and position concentration risk are elevated even in a decent P&L year.
insights.quote: it's gone down to 27 which actually to to Andrew's point I think it was um it suggests that at the moment there are very few markets that are trending.

insights.claim: 2026 year-to-date CTA gains have come mainly from equities, metals, and one or two currencies, not from broad-based participation across the futures universe that CTAs trade.
insights.speaker: Niels (host)
insights.so_what: Concentrated trend sources mean the strategy's diversification benefit this year is thinner than headline returns suggest.

insights.claim: The flagship CTA index is up roughly 23% over the trailing 12 months versus about 21% for MSCI World and about 2% for bonds, achieved with an equity beta of only around 0.3 — an unusually strong risk-adjusted outcome for a trend program.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: A 23% return at 0.3 beta is the kind of risk-adjusted number allocators should be citing when justifying a permanent (not just crisis-hedge) CTA allocation.

insights.claim: As of the update, the broad CTA index was up 58bps in August 2026 (+8.74% YTD) and the trend sub-index up 55bps (+8.5% YTD), while the short-term traders index was up 108bps in August (+4.3% YTD), and both MSCI World (+3.31% in August, +13.05% YTD) and the S&P 500 total return (+3.46% in August, +13.19% YTD) were outrunning CTAs on a YTD basis.
insights.speaker: Niels (host)
insights.so_what: In a low-crisis year, equities can outright beat trend strategies — a reminder that CTA allocations are a diversifier for tail risk, not a standalone equity-beating bet.

insights.claim: Going into August 2026, trend-following model portfolios flipped to short gold after a strong long-gold run earlier in the year and were generating positive P&L from the reversal.
insights.speaker: Tom Roble
insights.so_what: A CTA gold flip from long to short is a concrete, trackable signal of a regime change in the metals trend that discretionary macro investors can cross-check against their own gold thesis.

insights.claim: A 2026 yen intervention/reversal event caused far less CTA damage than expected — Andrew Beer says his firm actually outperformed through the event despite the yen having been one of the year's best money-making trades, and he admits he isn't fully sure why the damage was so contained.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Even a well-flagged intervention risk in a core CTA trade didn't produce the blowup allocators feared, suggesting current cross-market diversification within trend books is more robust than the 'single idiosyncratic shock' fear implies.

insights.claim: Andrew Beer's stated rule of thumb is that when an idiosyncratic shock hits a market a CTA is concentrated in (such as a short-yen trade unwinding on central-bank intervention), losses should be worse than the broad portfolio average — so the fact that didn't happen this time was itself an anomaly worth flagging to clients.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Investors should use this heuristic to size expected drawdowns whenever a CTA's largest position sits in a market facing acute policy/event risk.

insights.claim: A simultaneous long crude oil position offset losses during the yen/geopolitical shock, cushioning what otherwise looked like a 'nightmare scenario' of being long equities and long gold into a war-related event.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Illustrates the mechanism by which multi-market trend diversification blunts single-event tail risk — worth modeling explicitly rather than assuming crisis correlation always spikes.

insights.claim: In July 2026 the flagship hedge-fund-style CTA index underperformed while two UCITS-based CTA indices were up, a roughly 150bp gap that Andrew Beer attributes to possible undisclosed carry-trade exposure (e.g., yen carry) inside some hedge-fund CTA programs not present in UCITS structures.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: A large, unexplained monthly dispersion between vehicle types is a due-diligence flag — allocators should ask managers directly whether carry sleeves sit alongside pure trend books.

insights.claim: UCITS commodity trades settle P&L a couple of days later than index/ETF-based reporting, so comparing single-day CTA performance across UCITS versus hedge-fund vehicles during fast commodity moves is misleading; Tom Roble recommends rolling data into weekly periods to get stable cross-vehicle correlations.
insights.speaker: Tom Roble
insights.so_what: Analysts benchmarking CTA vehicles against each other should use weekly, not daily, return windows to avoid false signals from settlement-timing artifacts.

insights.claim: The historical mutual-fund versus hedge-fund CTA performance gap (US '40 Act funds underperformed by roughly 400-500bps in 2022 due to tighter volatility controls) has closed as providers like AQR, Alpha Simplex and Winton now run cleaner, lower-cost (roughly 100-150bp all-in) products, and the same convergence has now happened in the UCITS space too.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Vehicle-choice drag has largely disappeared, so allocators can now pick a CTA vehicle mainly on liquidity/tax/access grounds rather than expecting a structural return penalty.
insights.quote: they underperformed by 4 or 500 basis points in 2022 on the upside

themes.theme: Situational Awareness: An AI Fund's Near-Collapse

insights.claim: A highly leveraged, venture-style AI-focused fund referred to in the discussion as 'Situational Awareness' grew from roughly zero to about $45 billion in assets within a few years (with $20-25 billion cited as an intermediate figure), using leverage on the order of 4:1.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Illustrates how fast AI-themed leveraged vehicles can scale and how much collateral risk can build up in a very short window — a name allocators doing AI-exposure due diligence should be tracking.
insights.quote: 0 to 45 is it's it's a humbling number

insights.claim: The Situational Awareness fund was up over 300% through June 2026 before giving back roughly a third of those gains in July (one figure cited in the discussion put the July decline as high as 67%), and it still held Anthropic as one of its principal positions even after the drawdown.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: A fund that remains concentrated in one AI company after a violent drawdown is a case study in how quickly a triple-digit-return narrative can flip into a solvency scare.
insights.quote: you gave back a third of it in July and you still have Anthropic um you know as your one of your principal investments.

insights.claim: Andrew Beer argues no CTA in history has produced a drawdown resembling the Situational Awareness fund's because CTAs trade liquid listed futures where notional exposure can be sized and exited instantly, whereas the AI fund borrowed against illiquid private-company collateral that a lender can force-unwind — meaning 'leverage' means something structurally different in liquid futures versus private/venture-style credit.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Investors comparing CTA 'notional leverage' headlines to venture/private-credit leverage are conflating two very different risk profiles; the liquidity and collateral-forcing mechanism matters more than the leverage ratio itself.

insights.claim: Andrew Beer suggests some capital likely flowed into the Situational Awareness-style vehicle only after it was already up 200%+ for the year, drawing a parallel to the classic pattern of return-chasing flows arriving into Cathie Wood's ARK fund right before its collapse.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: A caution flag for any investor tempted to chase a headline-making, already-tripled AI vehicle late in its run.

themes.theme: Managed Accounts, Portable Alpha and Structural Evolution

insights.claim: The Standards Board for Alternative Investments (SBAI) published a guide on separately managed accounts (SMAs) laying out benefits including notional funding/capital efficiency (paying only margin), cross-margining across instruments, and — for multi-managers — cross-margining across allocations at the platform level, plus liquidity, transparency, customization and control advantages.
insights.speaker: Tom Roble
insights.so_what: Allocators evaluating SMA platforms now have an industry-standard reference document (SBAI's guide) to benchmark proposed terms against.

insights.claim: Investors are moving along a spectrum from using managed-account platforms that handle the operational heavy lifting, to more dedicated vehicles, to eventually building fully bespoke direct managed-account programs themselves — a heavier lift operationally but with maximum control.
insights.speaker: Tom Roble
insights.so_what: Gives allocators a roadmap for how to graduate from turnkey SMA platforms to fully custom infrastructure as their CTA allocation scales.

insights.claim: Portable alpha is thematic right now because it pairs naturally with managed accounts: an investor can overlay a CTA/diversifier position via listed derivatives on top of existing equity exposure (e.g., adding $20-50 of CTA exposure on top of $100 of equities) without diverting capital away from the equity book — effectively diversification without a separate capital outlay.
insights.speaker: Tom Roble
insights.so_what: This is the operating mechanism behind the current portable-alpha wave — a structure allocators can request from CTA managers to avoid an equity-vs-diversifier tradeoff.

insights.claim: Portable alpha has existed as a concept for roughly 30 years, yet has only become a mainstream industry talking point in the last two to three years — a timing gap Niels flags as itself worth investigating rather than assuming it's simply a new idea.
insights.speaker: Niels (host)
insights.so_what: Understanding why an old structure suddenly became fashionable (likely driven by SMA infrastructure maturing) helps allocators judge whether the trend is durable or a marketing cycle.

insights.claim: Andrew Beer argues CTAs ending up housed in a hedge-fund vehicle was 'almost a historical accident' — before the early 2000s, trend exposure was delivered through managed accounts for high-net-worth investors at firms like Dean Witter accessing traders such as John Henry and Campbell with heavy leverage, and the industry is now structurally reverting back toward managed accounts, mutual funds, UCITS, QIS and ETFs.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: The multi-decade vehicle cycle (managed account -> hedge fund -> managed account/ETF/UCITS) suggests the next wave of CTA product innovation will keep favoring capital-efficient, direct-access structures over commingled hedge funds.
insights.quote: it was almost a historical accident that CTAs ended up in a hedge fund vehicle in the first place.

insights.claim: Andrew Beer separates 'investment decisions' from 'vehicle/delivery decisions': he argues the industry has over-engineered the investment side for 25 years without moving the aggregate Sharpe ratio, but sees legitimate value in engineering the delivery side (low-cost products, UCITS access, ex-commodity versions, managed accounts) to expand the addressable investor base without changing the core signal.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: A useful due-diligence lens: judge a new CTA 'innovation' by whether it changes the signal (usually not worth paying up for) or just the wrapper (can genuinely expand access/efficiency).

insights.claim: Niels traces the term 'crisis alpha' back to a question posed to a researcher (referred to as Katy/KD) after 2008 about why these strategies do well in crises, with the answer resting on three properties: the strategies are unbiased, highly liquid, and opportunistic — not a marketing slogan invented after the fact.
insights.speaker: Niels (host)
insights.so_what: Knowing the original analytical basis for 'crisis alpha' helps investors separate the legitimate structural argument from the marketing overuse the panel criticizes later.

insights.claim: Andrew Beer's central critique of the 'crisis alpha' label: if the CTA index is priced at roughly cash + 250bps net of fees over 25 years and most of the excess return arrives in one big year every 8-10 years, then by construction the strategy is close to flat/cash-like most of the time — which is exactly what forces managers to market it as 'crisis alpha' since there's little else compelling to tell clients while they wait.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Reframes 'crisis alpha' marketing not as a strategic choice but as a symptom of a low-Sharpe product — investors should ask any CTA pitching 'crisis alpha' what its non-crisis-year Sharpe ratio actually is.
insights.quote: it's on cash plus 250 basis points net of fees and expenses, okay?

insights.claim: Andrew Beer's proposed fix isn't better marketing language but a materially higher Sharpe ratio: roughly doubling the excess-over-cash return generated in normal years (from about 20 points to about 40 points over a decade) is what actually converts a 'crisis alpha' product into something worth holding continuously rather than dead money between crises.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Gives allocators a concrete quantitative bar (roughly doubling non-crisis-year excess return) to judge whether a manager has genuinely earned an 'all-weather' positioning versus just relabeled the same low-Sharpe product.
insights.quote: you're not doing cumulatively 20 points over cash, you're doing 40 points over cash.

insights.claim: 'Risk Mitigating Strategies' (RMS) has emerged as the industry's newer rebrand of crisis alpha, but Tom Roble argues it's the same underlying concept — diversifying instruments that participate in growth periods while protecting in bad ones — and investors increasingly get frustrated when a short one-to-two-month equity drawdown isn't immediately offset by a 10-20% CTA gain, not appreciating that new trends take time to develop after a regime shift.
insights.speaker: Tom Roble
insights.so_what: Allocators should set realistic expectations for the lag between an equity shock and CTA protection materializing, rather than judging the strategy on a one-to-two-month window.

insights.claim: Andrew Beer dislikes the term 'trend following' itself, arguing the strategy's edge is not about being late into an established trend but about being very early when the first signs of a new trend emerge — he frames it as a 'completion strategy' for what most allocators structurally do badly, which is timing markets and abandoning losing convictions.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Reframes the manager pitch: the value proposition is disciplined regime-change detection and loss-cutting, not chasing momentum after the fact — a distinction worth using when explaining CTA allocations to skeptical committees.
insights.quote: it completion strategy for something that you as an allocator don't do well which is to time the markets.

insights.claim: Andrew Beer argues most real-world portfolios — sovereign wealth funds, wealth-management model portfolios, strategic asset allocations — barely move year to year despite market noise, so CTAs' true value-add is capturing the unexpected regime shifts that sit outside the range of those static allocations, a structural rather than cyclical source of edge.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Supports sizing CTA allocations based on how static an investor's core policy portfolio is, rather than on recent CTA performance alone.

themes.theme: Trend vs Non-Trend Classification and Manager Selection

insights.claim: The flagship CTA index provider has begun formally splitting its universe into 'CTA Trend' and 'CTA Non-Trend' categories because trend following itself is now well understood and widely accepted, while 'non-trend' remains a much less uniform, harder-to-define bucket.
insights.speaker: Tom Roble
insights.so_what: Allocators should ask index providers and managers which sub-index (trend vs non-trend) they're being benchmarked against, since blending the two obscures very different risk drivers.

insights.claim: Non-trend CTA sub-strategies break into roughly three groups: short-term trading (average holding period around 10 days/two weeks or less), quantitative/systematic macro (using forward-looking fundamental data rather than historical price data), and commodity-specialist quant strategies capturing directional or relative-value factors.
insights.speaker: Tom Roble
insights.so_what: A usable taxonomy for allocators to classify any 'non-trend CTA' pitch they receive into one of three genuinely distinct sub-strategies before evaluating it.

insights.claim: Short-term CTA strategies remain a structurally difficult business — Quest Partners returned capital in 2026, and Crabel is essentially the only billion-dollar-plus firm that has survived long-term purely in the short-term space, indicating high manager mortality in that niche.
insights.speaker: Tom Roble
insights.so_what: Short-term systematic strategies should be treated as a high-manager-risk allocation, not a safe complement to trend, given the sparse list of durable survivors.

insights.claim: Andrew Beer's blunt verdict on short-term/fast trend models: backtests look attractive because they imply earlier entries and later exits than slower trend, but in live trading the added whipsaws and overtrading turn it into 'a zero Sharpe ratio exercise' that erodes the apparent edge.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to any manager pitching fast/short-term signals as a superior version of trend — the backtest-to-live gap for speed is, in Beer's experience, consistently large.
insights.quote: It's a zero sharp ratio exercise.

insights.claim: Comparing the pure trend sub-index to the broader all-strategy CTA index shows essentially the same Sharpe ratio over time, which Andrew Beer reads as evidence that non-trend strategies (carry, short-term, macro) aren't adding meaningful diversification benefit at the index level despite being marketed as complementary.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Casts doubt on paying extra fees for 'non-trend diversifiers' bundled into a CTA program if the aggregate Sharpe ratio isn't actually improving versus pure trend.

insights.claim: A CTA source told Tom Roble that shorter-term strategies are often added less because they improve long-run return and more because they smooth the return profile enough that an allocator can keep presenting the product to an investment committee through volatile stretches — a business/optics rationale as much as an investment one.
insights.speaker: Tom Roble
insights.so_what: Investors should distinguish 'smoothing for optics' additions from genuine alpha-additive diversifiers when a manager explains why they blend in short-term sleeves.

insights.claim: Andrew Beer warns that risk controls, stop-losses, and short-term overlays that reduce drawdowns all carry a real economic cost by exiting positions before trends resume — some popular post-2022 US mutual fund launches added short-term 'protective' models after the late-2022 whipsaws, and subsequent performance shows that protection cost has been real, not free.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: A caution against buying 'smoother' CTA products marketed post-drawdown as protective upgrades — the smoothing mechanism itself may be a persistent drag on returns.

insights.claim: Niels and Tom Roble's practical manager-selection heuristic: institutional investors should hold two to four structurally different CTAs rather than a single manager, since single-manager selection risk is high and a genuinely diversified small basket captures the space's benefits without over-concentrating in one house's model.
insights.speaker: Niels (host)
insights.so_what: A directly actionable portfolio-construction rule allocators can apply immediately when building or reviewing a CTA sleeve.

insights.claim: Of the roughly 20 current constituents in the flagship CTA index, 17 have individually outperformed the index itself over the past decade, placing the index at only about the 15th percentile of return and the 35th percentile of Sharpe ratio versus its own current members — an optical illusion that makes manager selection look far easier than it is.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Any allocator comparing a single manager favorably to 'the index' should recognize the index is a deliberately conservative, diversification-weighted benchmark, not a typical constituent's return.
insights.quote: 17 of the 20 have outperformed the index over the past 10 years and the and so the socken CTA index would only be in the 15th percentile of the current managers

insights.claim: Only about 9 of the 20 CTA-index constituents from a decade ago are still in the index today, so allocators judging 'top managers' from the current constituent list are implicitly ignoring the roughly half of prior constituents that have since fallen out or shrunk into irrelevance.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Reinforces that today's index winners are not a stable, fixed set — due diligence should include what happened to the managers who dropped out, not just who's currently in.
insights.quote: if only nine of the 20 strategies 10 years ago are still around today

insights.claim: Efficient Capital's paper 'Blinded by Bias' documents that backfilling a CTA index using only its current constituents' full historical track records produces a materially stronger performance line than the true live, walk-forward version of the index.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Any 'index' or peer comparison built by backfilling current constituents' histories should be treated as inflated and discounted accordingly.
insights.quote: an excellent paper that um efficient capital have written about called blinded by bias

insights.claim: The index provider's practice of adding/removing constituents only prospectively — never restating history with new members' backfilled data — is, per Andrew Beer, the analytically correct approach, in contrast to older-generation hedge fund indices that used to backfill entire histories to make the index look better and compete on headline performance.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete methodology checkpoint to demand from any hedge fund index provider: no retroactive backfilling of new constituents' history.
insights.quote: that's like a cardinal sin from a statistical perspective

insights.claim: Andrew Beer coined the term 'sneaky selection bias' to describe how, because underperforming managers eventually drop out of the index and are replaced by managers who have recently done well, the index captures the negative performance of departing managers but never captures the positive lift of the replacement manager's earlier growth phase.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Explains a subtle structural downward bias in reported index returns that most allocators never account for when comparing manager performance to the benchmark.
insights.quote: you came up with this kind of term of sneaky bias, sneaky selection bias

insights.claim: Andrew Beer flags an unresolved measurement question: because roughly half of CTA index constituents report through managed-account composites that may exclude a cash/collateral return, rising interest rates could be silently understating the index's apparent return relative to what an all-in investable product would actually deliver.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: An open research question worth commissioning analysis on before assuming the published CTA index return is directly comparable across all constituent structures.

insights.claim: Pure long-only commodities have suffered roughly an 80% peak-to-trough drawdown over the past 25 years, versus a sub-20% max drawdown for the CTA space over the same period — the 'escalator up, elevator down' pattern in commodities is why they're typically capped at a small slice of institutional portfolios, even though investors mistakenly perceive CTAs as the riskier asset.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Corrects a common investor misperception: on realized drawdown history, diversified trend-following has been dramatically less risky than owning long-only commodities outright.
insights.quote: there's this expression about in commodities you take the escalator up and the elevator down.

insights.claim: Newer 'third-generation' systematic commodity funds combine trend, carry, and curve/term-structure roll-down strategies specifically to counter the structural roll cost of staying long a commodity curve continuously, aiming to deliver an inflation-hedge profile without the raw drawdown risk of pure long-only commodity exposure.
insights.speaker: Tom Roble
insights.so_what: Explains the design logic behind a growing category of commodity-only quant funds allocators should distinguish from both generic long-only commodity indices and generalist multi-asset CTAs.

insights.claim: Andrew Beer's own earlier venture (before his CTA-replication business) exploited large information asymmetries in thinly traded fundamental commodity markets, such as fixed-price natural gas forward contracts, where standard options-pricing theory broke down because supply/demand costs shifted in step functions across fuel sources (hydro to coal to gas) rather than following normal distributions.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Illustrates that fundamental commodity trading and systematic trend-following are structurally different edges (information asymmetry vs. price-based signal extraction), useful for allocators deciding whether to pair the two strategy types.

insights.claim: Tom Roble observes that markets appear to have 'forgotten' volatility despite an Iran-related war and ongoing geopolitical risk, with prices having digested the shock and equities resuming an upward drift — a sign of complacency risk building beneath a calm surface.
insights.speaker: Tom Roble
insights.so_what: A qualitative volatility-complacency read worth cross-checking against options-implied vol levels before assuming the current calm will persist.

insights.claim: Andrew Beer flags the SpaceX IPO and its associated multi-year 'fantastical' growth narrative as emblematic of a broader shift in how equity markets are being priced, comparing today's environment to a possible repeat of the 2000 dot-com top while acknowledging it could instead be genuinely different this time.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: A prominent trend-following practitioner explicitly raising a 2000-style top scenario is a signal worth weighing alongside more bullish AI-capex narratives when setting equity risk.
insights.quote: it could be a repeat of 2000 or it could be something very very different. But we just don't know at this point.

insights.claim: Andrew Beer describes today's public equity market as having absorbed venture-capital-style pricing logic (a 'one or two winners, killing field for everyone else' distribution) into mainstream large-cap names, a shift from his traditional-value-investing background that he says makes normal valuation analysis very difficult to apply right now.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Reinforces the case for rules-based trend exposure as a complement to discretionary equity analysis when fundamental valuation frameworks are becoming harder to apply.

insights.claim: Two competing macro narratives were simultaneously priced into CTA portfolios in 2026: an equity-side FOMO/AI-capex growth narrative and a more cautious narrative around a potential crude oil supply squeeze plus rising interest rates and stubborn inflation — both threads showed up as live positions in trend books rather than the market settling on one story.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: Explains why trend portfolios can hold seemingly contradictory macro bets (long equities and defensive commodity/rate exposure) at once — both narratives are being priced by different market segments simultaneously.

insights.claim: Andrew Beer notes that interest rate yields have been 'ticking higher and higher' in the background of 2026 without drawing much market attention, an underappreciated backdrop he flags alongside the more visible equity-market euphoria.
insights.speaker: Andrew Beer
insights.so_what: A quietly rising-yield backdrop combined with equity euphoria is a classic setup investors should watch for signs of eventual repricing risk.
